1.note: Ezekiel is using the phrase translated as **And it was** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

If your language would not represent numbers in forms such as **sixth** and **fifth**, you could represent these numbers in forms that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year six, in month six, on day five of the month]
Here, **to my face** represents “in front of me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [were sitting before me]

1.q: וַ⁠תִּפֹּ֤ל עָלַ⁠י֙ שָׁ֔ם יַ֖ד אֲדֹנָ֥⁠י יְהֹוִֽה
1.note: Here, **the hand of the Lord Yahweh** represents “the power of the Lord Yahweh.” By saying that it **fell**, Ezekiel means that the power of Yahweh came upon him in a special way so that he could see a vision. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And there the power of the Lord Yahweh came upon me so that I could see a vision]

2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **fire** is bright and blazing, so was the **likeness** that Ezekiel saw. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [a likeness that was bright and blazing like fire]

The word **fire** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, seems to imply that the entire figure was made of fire. The translators of the ancient Greek translation read this word with a different vowel, which would be “man.” You may want to follow this alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [a man]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4.

The word translated as **metal** refers to a kind of shining substance whose exact identity is uncertain. It could refer to: (1) a shiny metal, such as bronze. The ULT and UST follow this interpretation. (2) a shiny stone, such as amber. Alternate translation: [was like the eye of amber]

3.note: This could mean: (1) a **wind** that was sent in a special way by God, as in the ULT and UST, or (2) a spirit, probably God’s Spirit. Alternate translation: [the Spirit]
See how you translated the same expression, “visions of God,” in [1:1](ta:01).

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe an **image** that is characterized by **jealousy**, that is, an idol that caused Yahweh to be jealous. The phrase **the seat of** refers to the place where this idol had been set up. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the shrine for the idol that caused jealousy]

4.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to express his surprise at what he saw. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation as in the UST.

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the glorious light indicating that the God of Israel was present]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [2:1](ta:02).
See how you translated **Son of man** in [2:1](ta:02).

Yahweh is using **lift your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “look.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [now look]
See how you translated these same phrases in verse 4. Alternate translation: [and suddenly I saw that]

6.q: הֲ⁠רֹאֶ֥ה אַתָּ֖ה מ⁠הם עֹשִׂ֑ים תּוֹעֵב֨וֹת גְּדֹל֜וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בֵּֽית־יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל עֹשִׂ֣ים פֹּ֗ה לְ⁠רָֽחֳקָה֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל מִקְדָּשִׁ֔⁠י
6.note: Yahweh is using the question form to express his outrage at what the house of Israel is doing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am sure that you are completely outraged at what you are seeing that they are doing, the great abominations that the house of Israel is doing here, to be far from upon my sanctuary!]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:1](ta:03).

The phrase **to be far from upon my sanctuary** could mean: (1) the people are making themselves far from Yahweh’s sanctuary by doing these abominations. Not only are the Israelite’s hearts far from worshipping Yahweh, but he will remove them far from the sanctuary, as Ezekiel predicts in the first part of his book. Alternate translation: [so that they are far from worshipping me in my sanctuary] (2) the abominations the Israelites were doing in the temple would cause Yahweh to go far from his sanctuary. Ezekiel sees Yahweh do this in 10:18. Alternate translation: [so that I will have to leave my sanctuary]

Yahweh is using **you will yet return; you will see** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will see even more.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But you will see even more great abominations]
By **great**, here Yahweh means “very bad.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [very bad abominations]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the very horrible things…very horrible things]

7.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, who was transporting Ezekiel in his vision. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh brought]

Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to focus his readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and I saw something surprising there]

8.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to focus his readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and there it was]

9.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the evil, horrible things]
The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

10.note: The expression **carved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you must say who did the action, the context indicates that the Israelites had carved these images. Alternate translation: [that the Israelites had carved on the wall]

The word translated as **detestable thing** refers to any kind of animal that the Israelites were forbidden to eat. It was also used to refer to foreign gods that the Israelites were forbidden to worship. It may be intended to modify **beast**, or it may be a separate item, perhaps summarizing the previous two items. Alternate translation: [and beast, forbidden things] or [and detestable beast]

Ezekiel is repeating the word **around** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. It emphasizes that the carvings covered the walls everywhere. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [everywhere all around]

11.note: Here, **to their faces** represents “in front of them,” that is, in front of the carved images. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [were standing in front of the carved images]
The word **Jaazaniah** is the name of a man. He may have been one of the military commanders of King Zedekiah, mentioned in 2 Kings 25:23. The word **Shaphan** is the name of his father.

Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and each man had his censer in his hand]

12.q: הֲ⁠רָאִ֣יתָ בֶן־אָדָם֒ אֲשֶׁ֨ר זִקְנֵ֤י בֵֽית־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ עֹשִׂ֣ים בַּ⁠חֹ֔שֶׁךְ אִ֖ישׁ בְּ⁠חַדְרֵ֣י מַשְׂכִּית֑⁠וֹ
12.note: Yahweh is using the question form to express his outrage at what the elders of Israel are doing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am sure that you are completely outraged by seeing what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark—each man in the chambers of his carved image!]

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [For justification]

12.q: אֹמְרִ֗ים אֵ֤ין יְהוָה֙ רֹאֶ֣ה אֹתָ֔⁠נוּ עָזַ֥ב יְהוָ֖ה אֶת הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
12.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [they are saying that Yahweh does not see them and that he has abandoned the land]

13.note: Yahweh is using **you will yet return; you will see** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will see even more.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this in verse 6. Alternate translation: [But you will see even more great abominations]
By **great**, here Yahweh means “very bad.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [very bad abominations]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [horrible things]

14.note: Ezekiel is not referring to any specific **women** that he had mentioned before. He means that he saw some Israelite women there. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [some Israelite women]
The word **Tammuz** is the name of a (male) false god that people in Mesopotamia worshiped. People believed that this god died each year, and they wept to mourn for him.

15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to draw Ezekiel’s attention to what he is showing him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Son of man, look carefully at this!]

Yahweh is using **you will yet return; you will see** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will see even more.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this in verses 6 and 13. Alternate translation: [But you will see even more and greater abominations]
By **greater**, here Yahweh means “much worse.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [much worse abominations]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **abominations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [horrible things]

16.note: The implication is that by turning **their backs toward the temple of Yahweh**, these men were rejecting Yahweh in order to worship the sun. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their backs turned toward the temple of Yahweh in rejection of him]

17.note: Yahweh is using the question form to draw Ezekiel’s attention to what he is showing him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Son of man, look carefully at this!]

17.q: הֲ⁠נָקֵל֙ לְ⁠בֵ֣ית יְהוּדָ֔ה מֵ⁠עֲשׂ֕וֹת אֶת הַ⁠תּוֹעֵב֖וֹת אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָֽשׂוּ פֹ֑ה
17.note: Yahweh is using the question form for emphasis. He means that doing these abominations in his temple was not enough evil for **the house of Judah**, because they have also done other, more evil things. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The house of Judah did not consider that doing the abominations that they have done here was evil enough!]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:6.

Yahweh is speaking as if **violence** were a substance that could fill the land. He means that the people of Judah have done violent things everywhere in the land. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have done violent things everywhere in the land]

Yahweh is using **they have returned to make me angry** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they keep making me angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they make me angry over and over] or [they keep making me angry]

Yahweh is using **They are sending the branch out to their nose** as a common expression of the culture. The exact meaning of this expression is uncertain, but it basically refers to a gesture that is very insulting. Therefore, it means, “They are greatly insulting me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [thumbing their nose at me] or [greatly insulting me]

Some notes of ancient scribes suggest that the original phrase describing the insult was “to my nose” rather than **to their nose**. If so, in order to not write something insulting to God, the scribes who copied the Scriptures changed “my” to “their.” Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use either version of this expression. Alternate translation: [to my nose]

18.note: Yahweh is using the phrase **I will act in heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will act in anger] or [I will act furiously]

Yahweh is using **My eye** to represent himself as he looks at the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will not pity them]

Here, **in my ears** represents “to me,” meaning that they would call out to Yahweh intending that he would hear them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And they will call out to me]
By **great**, here Yahweh means “loud.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with a loud voice]

Yahweh is using **I will not hear them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will not respond to them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but I will not respond to them]
